frames.narration: A producer wants to append one record to a huge log file. It asks the master which chunk is the last one of the file and which chunkserver holds the lease for it. The master answers from its memory: it keeps the namespace, the file-to-chunk map and the chunk locations, and it holds less than 64 bytes for each 64 MB chunk.

The client caches the answer, so later appends skip the master. Now it pushes the record's data to the replicas. The data goes along a chain, from the client to the nearest chunkserver and on from one to the next, and each starts forwarding as soon as bytes arrive.

Once every replica has the data, the client sends the append request to the primary, which holds a lease from the master. The primary checks whether the record fits in the chunk. If not, it pads the chunk and tells the client to retry on the next chunk. Here it fits, so the primary picks the offset.
The primary writes the record at that offset and tells the secondaries to write it at the same offset, in the order it picked. This is the control flow, kept apart from the data flow.

The secondaries confirm, and the primary replies to the client with the offset. If any replica had failed, the client would retry, and some replicas might hold the record twice. Readers use unique ids and checksums to cope with that.

Later one secondary's machine dies. Its heartbeats stop, and the master finds every chunk that is down to two replicas. It clones them from surviving replicas, most endangered chunks first, at a limited speed so that applications are not slowed.

frames.narration: Every change to the namespace was written to the operation log, replicated on remote machines, before it was made visible. If the master restarts, it loads the latest checkpoint, replays the log, and asks the chunkservers which chunks they hold, because it never stored chunk locations.
